tweets.text:
According to Korean media reports, lead times for essential components used in semiconductor manufacturing equipment have more than doubled.

A senior executive at a Korean deposition equipment maker, identified as Company A, said, “We are struggling to secure components. We used to receive parts for deposition equipment within four months of placing an order, but that has recently stretched to as long as 10 months.”

Company B, which manufactures laser processing equipment for semiconductors, said it now takes up to 40 months to receive critical components from Japan.

“We are willing to pay a premium for faster delivery, but our component suppliers have told us they cannot shorten lead times because their production capacity is limited,” a Company B representative said. “Without alternative suppliers, we face immediate difficulties manufacturing equipment.”

Packaging equipment maker Company C has established a domestic component supply chain, but it is also experiencing delivery delays. “We are in a better position than companies sourcing from overseas, but securing components still takes about 50% longer than usual,” a Company C executive said.

That means components used to manufacture packaging equipment that typically arrived within four months now take six months or longer.

The industry’s reluctance to use Chinese components is also contributing to the problem amid U.S.-China trade tensions. There are concerns that including Chinese components in the supply chain for advanced semiconductor manufacturing could lead to restrictions on doing business with U.S. chipmakers. With Chinese suppliers having rapidly expanded their presence in the semiconductor equipment components market through competitive pricing, excluding them makes it difficult to find alternatives.

We view the report of a potential partnership between SK Hynix and Intel as highly credible. Through this alliance, SK Hynix can establish U.S.-based memory chip manufacturing capacity in a more efficient and cost-effective manner, swiftly aligning with "Made in USA" policy mandates and market demand. Compared to building a greenfield facility from scratch, this approach bypasses cumbersome regulatory approvals and avoids the prolonged lead times and heavy resource expenditure associated with land acquisition and power and water utility infrastructure.

Lightfield co-founder and CEO Keith Peiris on killing a product with two million monthly users and rebuilding the CRM from scratch:

Lightfield's predecessor was an AI presentation tool growing faster than the team could buy inference to support it. Keith shut it down anyway. Nobody on the team liked the product.

Keith decided he wanted to attack the CRM space, a vertical that's notoriously hard to break into. A company's record of its customers is scattered across a whole stack of systems that often contradict each other.

His bet is reconciling them into one coherent source of truth, what Lightfield calls a business world model. Every agent a team might run sits downstream of it.

In this conversation with a16z's Alex Rampell and Joe Schmidt: the office space they traded for their first 10 customers, why a CRM ended up modeled on the Facebook timeline, three attempts at pricing before one worked, and why nobody at a 40-person company has a fixed role.
